concept.technique_name: testing with suitable numerical values (AP and GP sums with common endpoints)

examples.problem_statement: A = a + A_1 + A_2 + \dots + A_N + b and B = a + G_1 + G_2 + \dots + G_N + b. A is the sum of n + 2 terms of an A.P. with first term a and last term b. B is the sum of n + 2 terms of a G.P. with first term a and last term b. What can be said about the relative values of A and B?

solution.operation: Choose a concrete G.P. with 6 terms: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32
solution.description: Instead of arguing in general, pick suitable values: fix a G.P. whose first and last terms will serve as the shared endpoints a and b.

solution.operation: Build the A.P. on the same endpoints: 1, 7.2, 13.4, 19.6, 25.8, 32
solution.description: Construct an A.P. with the same number of terms and the same first and last terms, so the two sums are compared on equal footing.
Add up the six A.P. terms to get the value of A for this instance.
Add up the six G.P. terms to get the value of B for the same endpoints.
Set the two sums side by side; the A.P. sum exceeds the G.P. sum, which settles the relative values.

key_reminders: For a 'compare in general' question with no constraint on a and b, a well-chosen concrete pair of sequences is enough to fix the relation.
The two sequences must share the same number of terms and the same first and last terms, or the comparison is not valid.
An A.P. is pinned down by its endpoints and term count via the common difference d = (b - a)/(n + 1).
common_mistakes: Picking an A.P. with a convenient whole-number difference instead of one that actually ends at 32, so the two sums no longer share endpoints.
Counting the terms wrongly: both sums here have n + 2 = 6 terms, including a and b themselves.

concept.technique_name: parity rules applied statement by statement

examples.problem_statement: If x is odd, which of the following must be true? Indicate all such statements. (A) x + 3 is even. (B) 2x is odd. (C) 3x + 1 is odd.

solution.result: \text{one fact to test against each of (A), (B), (C)}
solution.description: The problem supplies only the parity of x, so each statement has to be checked against that single fact.
Adding 3 to an odd value always lands on an even value, as the sample values confirm, so keep (A).
Multiplying any integer by an even number produces an even result, so 2x cannot be odd and (B) is eliminated.
Multiplying an odd integer by 3 keeps it odd, and adding 1 to an odd value makes it even, so 3x + 1 cannot be odd and (C) is eliminated.

key_reminders: odd + odd = even, so an odd x plus 3 is always even.
Any integer times an even number is even, whatever the parity of the integer.
odd times odd is odd, and odd + 1 is even.
common_mistakes: Reading 2x as odd because x is odd, forgetting that the even factor 2 decides the parity.
Stopping after 3x is odd in (C) and not carrying out the '+ 1', which flips the parity to even.

concept.technique_name: distance-rate-time applied leg by leg, then compared with a hypothetical trip

examples.problem_statement: Claudette travels the first 2/3 of a 60-mile trip at 20 miles per hour (mph) and the remainder of the trip at 30 mph. How many minutes later would she have arrived if she had completed the entire trip at 20 mph?

solution.description: Find the length of the first leg by taking two-thirds of the total 60-mile distance.
Divide the first leg's distance by its 20 mph rate to get the time spent on that leg, converted to minutes.
Subtract the first leg from the total to get the remaining distance travelled at the faster rate.
Divide the second leg's distance by its 30 mph rate to get the time spent on that leg, in minutes.
Add the two leg times to get the total duration of the trip as actually travelled.
Now price the hypothetical trip: cover the whole 60 miles at 20 mph to get its duration in minutes.
Subtract the real trip's time from the hypothetical one to see how much later she would have arrived.

key_reminders: time = distance / rate, applied separately to each leg because the rate changes partway.
Total time for a multi-rate trip is the sum of the leg times, never the distance divided by an averaged rate.
The question asks for minutes, so convert each hour figure (2 h, 2/3 h, 3 h) before comparing.
common_mistakes: Averaging 20 and 30 to 25 mph and computing 60/25, which ignores that more distance is covered at the slower rate.
Splitting the 60 miles into two 30-mile halves instead of the 2/3 and 1/3 split the problem specifies.
Reporting the hypothetical trip's 180 minutes rather than the 20-minute difference the question asks for.
